question: A 52-year-old man on ramipril for hypertension develops a persistent dry cough. Which mechanism best explains this adverse effect?

answers.text: Accumulation of bradykinin in the respiratory mucosa due to ACE inhibition

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. ACE degrades bradykinin; inhibition of ACE leads to bradykinin accumulation in bronchial tissue, stimulating cough-receptor fibres. This occurs in 10–15% of patients and is class-specific to ACEi.
Incorrect. Hyperkalaemia (a real ACEi side effect) does not cause cough; it manifests as cardiac dysrhythmias.

answers.text: Angiotensin II receptor overstimulation at AT2 receptors

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. ACEi reduces Ang II formation, so AT2 stimulation actually decreases — and is not the cough mechanism.

answers.text: Direct irritant effect of ramipril on the tracheal mucosa

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The cough is not a local irritant effect; it is mediated by systemic bradykinin accumulation and is abolished by switching to an ARB (which does not inhibit ACE).

overallFeedback.feedback: ACE (kininase II) degrades bradykinin. ACE inhibition → bradykinin accumulation → cough. ARBs block Ang II receptors but do not affect ACE, so they do not cause this side effect.

Correct. ACE inhibits the breakdown of bradykinin — the same enzyme that converts Ang I to Ang II. Bradykinin accumulation in the airway triggers afferent C-fibre stimulation and cough in ~10–15% of patients. Switching to an ARB resolves the cough.
